title: Sugar Queen and the Blind Bandit
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 3 of 40
content:
Katara and Toph could turn buying nails into a moral disagreement.

We needed supplies for a temporary footbridge in the eastern district. That should have been simple: lumber, fasteners, rope, two metal brackets, and enough patience to survive the market.

The problem was that Katara believed lists were sacred.

Toph believed lists were what happened when people distrusted instinct.

I believed both of them should be banned from choosing lunch.

“We are not buying from him,” Katara said.

The hardware merchant froze halfway through wrapping a bundle of nails.

Toph tilted her head. “Why not?”

“Because he charged the woman before us less.”

“He likes her better.”

“He thinks we’re tourists.”

“He thinks you’re a tourist.” Toph jerked a thumb toward herself. “I’m delightful.”

“You threatened to bend his sign into a hat.”

“It was ugly.”

I put both hands over my face.

The merchant cleared his throat. “Perhaps I could offer—”

“The original price,” Katara said.

“Or the hat,” Toph added.

We got the original price.

Outside, Katara was still annoyed.

“It’s the principle.”

Toph balanced the box of nails on one shoulder. “You have too many principles. They’re crowding the place.”

“And you don’t have enough.”

“I have one. Don’t be boring.”

They walked on opposite sides of me like rival weather systems.

I had known them for less than a month and already understood that their arguments were not signs of dislike. They fought because neither of them knew how to care quietly.

Katara cared by noticing what was unfair and refusing to let it pass.

Toph cared by treating everyone she loved as sturdy enough to survive honesty.

Both methods could be exhausting.

Both had saved lives.

We stopped at a tea stall. Katara ordered jasmine. Toph ordered something strong enough to “taste like it had survived a landslide.” I ordered whatever would prevent murder.

Toph set her bare feet against the packed-earth floor and turned her face toward me.

“You’re staring.”

“I am not.”

“Your breathing changed.”

Katara sighed into her tea. “Toph.”

“What? I’m helping.”

“No one has ever said that after you announced someone’s heartbeat.”

Toph grinned. “Cowards.”

Heat climbed my neck.

The truth was I had been watching Katara’s hands.

She moved with extraordinary economy. Even resting, her fingers seemed ready to shape water. There were tiny scars across her knuckles. A pale line crossed the heel of one palm. These were not the hands of the serene healer people described in speeches. They were working hands.

Toph slapped the table.

“There it is again.”

I nearly choked on my tea.

Katara’s eyes widened, then narrowed at Toph. “Leave them alone.”

“Oh, you don’t know what I’m talking about?”

“I know exactly what you’re doing.”

Toph leaned back. “Then why are you blushing?”

Katara looked at me.

I looked at the tea.

The tea failed to open and swallow me.

Toph cackled.

“Someday,” I told her, “I’m going to learn to lie so well you can’t tell.”

“Nope.”

“I hate your confidence.”

“You like my confidence.”

That was worse.

Katara rescued me by changing the subject. “The bridge.”

“Yes,” I said immediately. “Wood. Nails. Blessedly unromantic infrastructure.”

Toph made a thoughtful noise. “You’d be surprised.”

“Don’t.”

We carried the supplies toward the river.

The temporary bridge connected two neighborhoods divided by a canal widened for factory barges. Children crossed it for school. Workers crossed it for the night shift. The old wooden span had rotted faster than anyone admitted.

Toph knelt at one support and pressed her fingertips to the stone.

“This footing’s garbage.”

“Can you fix it?” I asked.

“Obviously.”

Katara set down the rope. “We’re rebuilding both sides.”

“We don’t need both.”

“We do if we want it to last through spring flood.”

Toph frowned. “Water people always think water is going to win.”

“Water usually does.”

“Not against a mountain.”

“Give me enough time.”

I laughed.

Toph’s face turned toward Katara. “See? Paperwork gets it.”

“Paperwork has a name,” Katara said.

The defense warmed me more than it should have.

Toph’s expression shifted, almost imperceptibly.

“Yeah,” she said. “I know.”

Then she used my name.

Just once.

No teasing attached.

It landed strangely.

We worked until late afternoon. Toph raised new stone footings while Katara redirected the current around them. I measured planks, kept children away from the work zone, and argued with a foreman who insisted the city had not authorized us to close the crossing.

“The Avatar authorized it,” he said when I produced the order.

“No,” I replied. “The municipal office did. Aang just signed because your office ignored us for three weeks.”

Toph’s grin from ten feet away was so smug I could feel it.

When the last brace was set, Katara stepped onto the bridge and bounced once.

“Solid.”

Toph looked offended. “Of course it’s solid.”

Katara smiled. “I was complimenting you.”

“Oh.”

Toph’s shoulders changed. Barely. A softening no one would notice if they did not know to look.

“I knew that,” she said.

Katara reached out and squeezed her forearm.

Toph did not pull away.

There was history in that touch.

Not romance, necessarily. Not yet. But something layered: old fights beside campfires, shared danger, nights when Katara had probably worried and Toph had pretended not to need it. Their closeness did not resemble Aang and Katara’s. It was rougher. Less named.

I wondered how many kinds of love could exist in one group before people stopped trying to sort them.

Toph’s head turned sharply toward me.

“Nope.”

“What?”

“I don’t know what you’re thinking, but your heart just did something annoying.”

Katara laughed.

I kicked a pebble off the bridge.

We sat on the riverbank while the first people crossed.

Katara took off her boots and let her feet rest in the water. Toph sat with hers planted in the mud. I stretched my legs between them.

For once, nobody argued.

The evening light turned the water copper.

Katara leaned back on her hands. “Toph.”

“Yeah?”

“Thank you for coming.”

“You would’ve built it wrong.”

“Toph.”

A pause.

“You’re welcome, Sugar Queen.”

Katara bumped her shoulder against Toph’s.

Toph returned it hard enough to nearly knock her into the river.

Katara grabbed Toph’s arm and pulled.

Toph yelped.

“Don’t you dare—Katara, I swear—”

They both went into the shallow water.

Toph screamed insults so inventive that three children stopped on the bridge to listen.

Katara laughed until she could barely stand.

I laughed with her.

Then Toph planted both hands in the muddy bank and launched a sheet of wet earth at us.

The next five minutes became war.

When Aang finally arrived, carrying dinner and looking delighted by the disaster, he found the three of us soaked, muddy, and breathless.

“What happened?”

Katara pointed at Toph.

Toph pointed at Katara.

I said, “Infrastructure.”

Aang stared at us.

Then he sat down on the bank and laughed so hard he dropped the dumplings.

That night, after I scrubbed mud from my clothes, I found one small river stone in my pocket.

Smooth. Flat. Warm from having been carried against me.

I set it on the table beside my bed.

I did not know which of them I was thinking about when I smiled.

That was becoming the problem.

The sugar sculpture survived exactly one day.

Toph found it in my room while looking for a tool she insisted I had borrowed. I had not borrowed it. She had left it in my coat pocket during the market trip and forgotten.

“You kept this?” she asked.

I turned from the window. “It was a gift.”

“It was a weapon.”

“It was a flower.”

“It could be both.”

She held the brittle little shape between two fingers. Katara had twisted the hot sugar into something that looked like a water lily if viewed generously. Toph had contributed by declaring it structurally unsound and then strengthening the stem with a sliver of metal so thin I had not noticed it.

“You helped make it,” I said.

“I prevented collapse. Different thing.”

The words landed differently after weeks of watching the two of them argue over everything from nails to noodles. Katara pushed. Toph resisted. Katara worried. Toph pretended concern was an insult. Somewhere between them, things did not collapse.

Toph set the sugar flower back on the table with exaggerated care.

“You’re thinking too loudly.”

“That isn’t a real thing.”

“Your heartbeat says otherwise.”

I hated that she could do that.

“What am I thinking?”

She smirked. “Not telling you for free.”

“Extortion.”

“Business.”

I threw the missing tool at her. She caught it without looking.

At the door she paused.

“Sugar Queen likes you,” she said.

My stomach dropped.

Toph’s grin sharpened. “And there it is.”

Then she left me alone with a sugar flower, a metal stem, and absolutely no ability to pretend my problem involved only one person.

The next morning, the sugar flower had cracked along one petal. The metal stem held. I decided that counted as symbolism only if nobody told Toph.
